facts.claim: Noise-cancelling headphones use a microphone on the ear cup to listen to outside noise and report it to the circuitry.
spoken: Tiny microphones on each ear cup listen to the noise outside

facts.claim: The circuitry generates an inverted (180-degree out-of-phase, antiphase) copy of the noise and plays it through a speaker.
spoken: A chip flips that wave upside down
and plays it through a speaker into your ear

facts.claim: Where the noise wave is at a peak the anti-noise is at a trough, so they sum to (near) zero: destructive interference.
spoken: so every peak becomes a valley
When the waves meet, peak plus valley adds up to flat

facts.claim: ANC is most effective at low frequencies; steady, constant, repetitive noise such as engine rumble or ventilation is easier to cancel than sudden, random sound.
facts.value: low, steady, repeating noise cancels best
spoken: It works best on steady, low rumbles, like engines and ventilation, because they repeat and the chip can predict them

facts.claim: Sudden sounds and high-frequency noise are hard for ANC to track; passive isolation (physical blocking by the cushions) is what handles them.
facts.value: sudden / high-pitched sound is blocked physically
spoken: A sudden clap changes too fast, so the cushions have to block it instead

facts.claim: Pitch-of-a-jet-engine illustration: ANC headphones make a loud steady jet-engine drone much quieter (noise reduction, not total silence).
facts.caveat: illustrative: ANC reduces, not eliminates, engine noise (freeCodeCamp: not total silence)
spoken: A jet engine roars, and you barely hear it
So the quiet you hear is sound fighting sound
